newsitem.title: GERMANY: Intel -weak Europe demand to continue in H2.
newsitem.headline: Intel -weak Europe demand to continue in H2.

text.p: Intel Corp said on Wednesday it expected European growth to continue to lag in the second half after trailing behind the chip maker's worldwide sales increases in the first half of 1997.
"I think Europe, at least in the third and fourth quarters, will not be gangbusters," said Hans Geyer, Intel vice president for Europe.
Second-quarter sales in Europe rose only three percent to $1.43 billion -- well off the company's worldwide sales growth rate of 29 percent.

Worldwide sales totaled $5.959 billion, as American sales surged 42 percent to $2.622 billion, Japanese sales rose 40 percent to $775 million and Asian-Pacific sales climbed 36 percent to $1.132 billion.
Technology analysts said rivals Advanced Micro Devices Inc and Cyrix Corp were winning over some of Europe's larger sellers of consumer PCs.
"There has been a lot of activity for the other chip makers," said James Bates at Context in London. "AMD and Cyrix have seen good growth on the consumer side.

Compaq Compter Corp has begun using a Cyrix chip in its home PCs, as has IBM Corp, which manufacturers chips for Cyrix. Fujitsu's PC unit, as well as top German retailer Vobis Microcomputer AG, have gone with AMD in a variety of product lines.
Geyer blamed weak European demand on an inventory problem stemming from a broad transition and the continent's hesitation in adopting new technology.
The inventory of standard Pentium chips has not moved out yet but production of those products ended in June, he said.
In their place Intel was making a major transition to Pentium processors with MMX multimedia technology and its latest iteration, the Pentium II processor.
But Intel was not sure if even the new chips would speed up the rate at which Europe buys new computer technology. "This is absolutely a concern," Geyer said.
Market researchers estimate 53 percent of Europe's white collar workers use PCs, compared to 90 percent in the U.S.
Geyer said rivals Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Cyrix Corp. were not putting price pressure on Intel, adding that Pentium II maintained the company's lead in processor performance.
Pentium II chips should make up about a quarter of Intel's total output by the end of the year and half of its production around the middle of 1998.

A new 0.25-micron manufacturing process due to begin in four plants in the autumn and winter would enable Intel to make Pentium II chips that run at 300 megaherz and beyond. This process would more than double its Pentium II capacity, Geyer said.
Second-quarter sales in Europe fell short of the first-quarter's total, as did sales in the Asia-Pacific region. Sales in Japan and America rose sequentially, the company said.
In May Intel warned that second-quarter results would not exceed those of the first quarter, blaming weak demand in Europe, where economic uncertainty has dampened PC sales.
Intel's second quarter net income rose 58 percent to $1.645 billion.
